But recent wartime energy disruptions are far from the only source of price pressures. Inflation has now exceeded the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. And looking ahead, inflation appears set to trend meaningfully above that target. Excess inflation is unacceptable. It hurts families, businesses, taxpayers and the American economy. Congress charged the FOMC with delivering price stability as well as maximum employment. We must fulfill this responsibility. In my remarks today, I’ll describe my outlook for economic activity, employment and inflation, then discuss how I believe monetary policy should adjust to sustainably achieve both of the FOMC’s mandated goals. These are my views and not necessarily those of my FOMC colleagues. [OFFICIAL] activity and employment [OFFICIAL] growth is strong.

Monetary policy, however, addresses cyclical mismatches between supply and demand, not structural challenges such as employers’ uncertainties. And the latest data show hints of increased dynamism, including more job openings and more workers quitting their jobs. My assessment is that the economy is achieving maximum employment and, supported by strong aggregate demand, remains on track to continue to do so. Inflation Turning to price stability, the FOMC targets an annual inflation rate of 2 percent as measured by the PCE price index. It’s important to know what it means to target an inflation rate. In my travels around the region, I’ve learned a lot about the remarkable technologies that make the energy industry so productive. One of those is directional and horizontal drilling.

Metrics that remove volatile categories or extreme price changes provide better signals of where overall inflation is likely to trend. For example, core PCE inflation excludes food and energy prices, which have relatively little predictive power for future overall inflation. Core PCE inflation was 3.1 percent over the 12 months through September. The Consumer Price Index for October came out this morning. It was higher than expected. I am concerned that PCE inflation could rise when we receive those data for October in a couple of weeks. Other measures that filter out volatile or extreme price changes likewise indicate inflation is trending meaningfully above 2 percent target. The [OFFICIAL] Fed’s multivariate core trend inflation index registered 2.8 percent in September.

Inflation also remains somewhat elevated in manufactured goods affected by tariffs. But the pressures are broader than that. Prices for non-housing, non-transportation core services rose 3.2% over the 12 months ended in September. That increase is eight tenths of a percentage point above the pace that has historically been consistent with achieving the FOMC’s inflation target. Non-housing, non-transportation core services include categories like visits to the doctor, childcare, dining out and hotel stays. Prices for these services aren’t particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips. While I expect inflation to moderate as price pressures dissipate in energy and manufactured goods, the broader inflationary trend is more likely to persist. Monetary policy When inflation trends too high while the labor market remains near maximum employment and even tightens, the FOMC is achieving only one of its two goals.

Tighter policy will be necessary to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for inflation and employment. And it is important to achieve that balance promptly. The longer above-target inflation persists, the greater the risk that it becomes baked into behavior. The CEO of a major global manufacturer talked with me recently about his thinking on wage increases for 2027. This CEO grew up working class. He knows what rising gas and grocery bills can do to a family. So, he leans toward raising pay in 2027 to offset the inflation in 2026. Across the economy, nominal wage growth has been subdued the past few years. That kept inflation from being even higher but also meant some workers’ pay fell behind the cost of living.

An approach like this CEO described could take some pressure off workers. But if it became widespread, the FOMC would have to slow the economy more to bring inflation back to target. The FOMC should not take that risk. In my view, accommodative monetary policy is adding to inflationary pressures. Economists have a concept called the neutral interest rate that measures the level where the fed funds rate is neither supporting nor restraining activity. The neutral rate is uncertain. It cannot be directly observed, but it can be estimated with economic models. Across eight published models, estimates of the neutral real interest rate currently range from 1 to 1.85 percent. The fed funds rate is 3.88 percent in nominal terms.

To convert that to a real rate, you have to subtract off expected inflation. My staff examined a baker’s dozen surveys measuring inflation expectations over the next year among households, businesses and market participants. The data suggest respondents expect PCE inflation to run around 3.1 percent in the near term, up a percentage point from before the pandemic. That makes the real fed funds rate 78 basis points, or a quarter-percentage-point below the lowest estimate of neutral. Moreover, broad financial conditions are currently providing a tailwind to the economy. As I said earlier, stocks have risen this year. Credit spreads widened this fall but remain compressed by historical standards. Banks remain eager to lend. Long-term interest rates have risen significantly so far in 2026, about three-quarters of a percentage point on net in the case of 10-year Treasury notes.

But those higher long-term rates do not represent as much of a drag on the economy as you might expect. Rates rose mainly because investors expect stronger nominal growth and higher neutral interest rates. So, the higher market rates are more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity. There are always risks to the economic outlook. Escalation or de-escalation of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East could change the path of energy prices, with implications for inflation and demand. Business investment could strengthen or falter as companies learn more about the uses of artificial intelligence and governments consider policies toward this potentially transformative technology. Fiscal policy may change with a new Congress.

And forecasts of inflation and employment are just forecasts. They come with uncertainty, and as a policymaker, I’m humble about my ability to predict the future. But policymakers must make decisions in the face of uncertainty, with the information we have available. I anticipate that without any monetary policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur. I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target. After raising the fed funds target range by 25 basis points in September, the FOMC skipped an increase at our October meeting. [OFFICIAL] markets had been volatile in the weeks before the meeting in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments.

In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary. Moreover, as long as market participants understand the FOMC’s policy plans, the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay. Skipping one meeting does not change the monetary policy destination. Indeed, by making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip. It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases. The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment.

It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall. After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate. The goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive so we can sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices. Market- and survey-based measures of long-run inflation expectations are near 2 percent, indicating the public trusts the FOMC to deliver price stability. By communicating and delivering on a strategy for moving to a modestly restrictive stance, the Fed can continue to earn that trust. Of course, I will change my policy views if the economic outlook and risks change.
